newsitem.title: UK: US tobacco prosecutor advises Britain to sue.
newsitem.headline: US tobacco prosecutor advises Britain to sue.

text.p: The lawyer who helped coordinate the state of Florida's lawsuit against tobacco companies on Thursday urged Britain's National Health Service to press its own lawsuits.

Tim Howard said he would tell directors of NHS trusts -- the government-contracted operators of local health services -- that the tobacco industry had intentionally addicted British citizens and passed on the health costs to the NHS.
"It's time for that to stop," Howard told BBC radio.

"The health authorities are already having enough trouble meeting demands for regular citizens and because of the cost of the disease, your citizens are having to wait for months and months to get proper treatment."
More than 30 U.S. states joined forces after pressing their own individual lawsuits against the tobacco companies to recoup the costs of caring for sick smokers.

Earlier this month they made a provisional settlement with the tobacco companies calling for them to pay $368.5 billion, some of which would be earmarked for anti-smoking and public health programmes.
Howard said the NHS trusts should do the same.
"This is an opportunity for a united front, similar to what has taken place...in America," he said. "We brought the tobacco companies to their knees in America," he added.
Howard, who is speaking to a meeting of the trusts in the southern resort town of Brighton, said a suit would involve little risk.

"The cost to health trusts would be minuscule, number one. Number two, the evidence to show the conspiracy to addict your citizens and transfer the costs to them have been developed in the U.S.," he said.
"They won't have to pay a dime. In England the prevailing party gets their fees paid for and in this trial the health trusts would clearly (win)."
Howard said smoking was not a matter of free choice.

"The reality is that 90 percent of your smokers begin in their teens. Sixty percent in America begin by the time they're 14. None of these children are aware that nicotine is as addictive as cocaine and heroin," he said.
He also denied he was out to drive the tobacco companies out of business. "The reality is they're impossible to run out of business," he said.

"What we want is...for them to pay for the disease they cause, number one, and number two we want them to take the addictive nature out of their cigarettes -- take the nicotine out and see if people want to put poison in their lungs. I daresay they won't."
The NHS trusts have said they were considering suing.
Sandy Macara, chairman of the British Medical Association, has also urged the trusts to sue. British legal experts say they, as well as private medical insurers, have a good case.
